person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: THE COMPETING QUANTITATIVE DEFINITIONS OF `FAIRNESS` THEMSELVES - catalogued, put into one notation, and then shown to be mutually unsatisfiable
span.quote: The rapid growth of this new field has led to wildly inconsistent motivations, terminology, and notation, presenting a serious challenge for cataloging and comparing definitions. This article attempts to bring much-needed order.

span.label: what the definitions of algorithmic fairness are, what each one assumes, and whether they can be held together
span.quote: The goal of this article is not to advance axiomatic definitions of fairness but to summarize the definitions and results in this area that have been formalized to date.

span.label: a notationally consistent catalogue of fairness definitions, the choices and assumptions each rests on, and the impossibility results that separate them
span.quote: Although each flavor of fairness definition presented in this section formalizes an intuitive notion of fairness, these definitions are not mathematically or morally compatible in general. In this section, we review several impossibility results about definitions of fairness

span.label: critique
span.quote: Much of the subsequent conversation consisted of either trying to harmonize these definitions of fairness or asserting that one or the other is correct. As it turns out, there can be no harmony among definitions in a world where inequality and imperfect prediction are the reality.

span.label: a young field in which one word carries several formal meanings that cannot all be satisfied at once, so that two competing analyses of the same tool can both be arithmetically correct
span.quote: Their most discussed finding was that COMPAS does not satisfy equal false positive rates by race: Among defendants who did not get rearrested, black defendants were twice as likely to be misclassified as high risk. Based largely on this and other similar findings, they described the tool as biased against blacks. Northpointe (now Equivant), the developers of COMPAS, critiqued ProPublica's work and pointed out that COMPAS satisfies equal positive predictive values: among those called higher risk, the proportion of defendants who got rearrested is approximately the same regardless of race (Dieterich et al. 2016). COMPAS also satisfies calibration within groups

span.label: a review: collect the published definitions, restate them in one notation, and set the impossibility theorems against the public COMPAS dispute as a worked case
span.term: a review: collect the published definitions, restate them in one notation, and set the impossibility theorems against the public COMPAS dispute as a worked case
span.quote: The goal of this article is not to advance axiomatic definitions of fairness but to summarize the definitions and results in this area that have been formalized to date.

span.label: THE INCOMPATIBILITY IS NOT A PROPERTY OF ALGORITHMS. `The trade-off between different notions of fairness WOULD APPLY EVEN IF A HUMAN WERE THE ONE MAKING THE PREDICTION`, and `REJECTING MODEL-DRIVEN OR AUTOMATED DECISION-MAKING IS NOT A WAY TO AVOID THESE PROBLEMS`. It is a property of predicting at all, under inequality
span.quote: Notably, scholars have emphasized that the trade-off between different notions of fairness would apply even if a human were the one making the prediction (Kleinberg et al. 2016). Rejecting model-driven or automated decision-making is not a way to avoid these problems.

span.label: and the conditions under which the definitions COULD agree are named and are both unreachable: equal base rates or perfect prediction. The paper calls them `trivial, degenerate, OR EVEN UTOPIAN (REPRESENTING TWO VERY DIFFERENT UTOPIAS)`
span.quote: Equal base rates and perfect prediction can be called trivial, degenerate, or even utopian (representing two very different utopias).

span.label: the paper declines the job most readers want done: `THE GOAL OF THIS ARTICLE IS NOT TO ADVANCE AXIOMATIC DEFINITIONS of fairness BUT TO SUMMARIZE the definitions and results ... FORMALIZED TO DATE`. It catalogues a disagreement rather than settling it, and says so in the introduction
span.quote: The goal of this article is not to advance axiomatic definitions of fairness but to summarize the definitions and results in this area that have been formalized to date.

span.label: and it names the gap its own subject cannot close: `GAPS BETWEEN MATHEMATICALLY CONVENIENT FORMALISM AND THE LARGER SOCIAL GOALS that many of these concepts were introduced to address`. THAT IS THE OPERATIONALISATION GAP, NAMED AS SUCH, by a paper whose subject is operationalisations
span.quote: Alongside this summary, we point out gaps between mathematically convenient formalism and the larger social goals that many of these concepts were introduced to address.

span.label: the object being predicted is already an abstraction of the thing anyone cares about: policy goals are `SOMETIMES CLUMSILY, ABSTRACTED AND FORMULATED TO FIT INTO A PREDICTION TASK`, and the choices that do it sit outside the model
span.quote: Several recent papers have demonstrated how policy goals are, sometimes clumsily, abstracted and formulated to fit into a prediction task (Dobbe et al. 2018, Eckhouse et al. 2018, Green 2018, Green & Hu 2018, Ochigame et al. 2018, Silva & Kenney 2018, Passi & Barocas 2019, Selbst et al. 2019). In this section, we link these concerns to choices and assumptions made in the policy design process.

span.label: and the decision itself is flattened before any of this begins: a judge's options are many, `IN THIS LITERATURE, THIS DECISION IS OFTEN REDUCED TO A BINARY DECISION - RELEASE OR DETAIN`. Every fairness metric in the catalogue is defined over that binary
span.quote: Although the options available to judges are many (including simply releasing the person, setting bail, requiring participation in a supervised release program, etc.), in this literature, this decision is often reduced to a binary decision—release or detain.

span.label: the authors record the standing criticism of their own field without dismissing it: quantitative notions of fairness `can FUNNEL OUR THINKING INTO NARROW SILOS where we aim to make adjustments to a decision-making process, RATHER THAN to address the STRUCTURAL CONDITIONS that sustain inequality in society`
span.quote: Recent criticisms of this line of work have rightly pointed out that quantitative notions of fairness can funnel our thinking into narrow silos where we aim to make adjustments to a decision-making process, rather than to address the structural conditions that sustain inequality in society

span.label: whether the incompatibility is an artefact of using algorithms at all
span.note: eliminates: the algorithmic explanation - the trade-off `would apply EVEN IF A HUMAN WERE THE ONE MAKING THE PREDICTION`, so refusing automation does not avoid it · outcome: held
span.quote: Notably, scholars have emphasized that the trade-off between different notions of fairness would apply even if a human were the one making the prediction (Kleinberg et al. 2016). Rejecting model-driven or automated decision-making is not a way to avoid these problems.

span.label: under what conditions the two COMPAS criteria COULD both hold, worked out formally
span.note: eliminates: any hope of reconciliation in practice - it requires equal recidivism rates across racial groups, or a group that never experiences an outcome, or perfect prediction · outcome: held
span.quote: Putting this in context and recalling that sufficiency implies equality of positive predictive values and that separation implies equality of false positive rates, this result shows that both supported definitions of fairness in the COMPAS debate can only be met when (a) the rate of recidivism and the distribution of scores are the same for all racial groups or (b) there are some groups that never experience some of the outcomes

span.label: whether formal fairness work is worth doing at all, against its own critics
span.note: eliminates: nothing on either side, and the paper says so: the criticisms are `rightly pointed out`, and formalism `SHOULD NOT BE DISMISSED as necessarily preserving the status quo`. Both are asserted; neither is tested · outcome: partial
span.quote: Recent criticisms of this line of work have rightly pointed out that quantitative notions of fairness can funnel our thinking into narrow silos where we aim to make adjustments to a decision-making process, rather than to address the structural conditions that sustain inequality in society

span.label: algorithmic fairness
span.quote: Though the algorithmic fairness conversation is somewhat new, it resembles older work. For example, since the 1960s, psychometricians have studied the fairness of educational tests based on their ability to predict performance

span.label: equal false positive rates
span.quote: Their most discussed finding was that COMPAS does not satisfy equal false positive rates by race: Among defendants who did not get rearrested, black defendants were twice as likely to be misclassified as high risk. Based largely on this and other similar findings, they described the tool as biased against blacks. Northpointe (now Equivant), the developers of COMPAS, critiqued ProPublica's work and pointed out that COMPAS satisfies equal positive predictive values: among those called higher risk, the proportion of defendants who got rearrested is approximately the same regardless of race (Dieterich et al. 2016). COMPAS also satisfies calibration within groups

span.label: sufficiency
span.quote: Putting this in context and recalling that sufficiency implies equality of positive predictive values and that separation implies equality of false positive rates, this result shows that both supported definitions of fairness in the COMPAS debate can only be met when (a) the rate of recidivism and the distribution of scores are the same for all racial groups or (b) there are some groups that never experience some of the outcomes

span.label: bias
span.quote: In recent years, attention has focused on how consequential predictive models may be biased—a now overloaded word that, in popular media, has come to mean that the model's performance (however defined) unjustifiably differs along social axes such as race, gender, and class.

span.label: quantitative notions of fairness
span.quote: Recent criticisms of this line of work have rightly pointed out that quantitative notions of fairness can funnel our thinking into narrow silos where we aim to make adjustments to a decision-making process, rather than to address the structural conditions that sustain inequality in society

Northpointe: it `SATISFIES EQUAL POSITIVE PREDICTIVE VALUES` and calibration within groups. NEITHER SIDE MISCALCULATED. They used different definitions of the same word

span.label: the formal conditions for agreement, stated exactly: SUFFICIENCY implies equality of positive predictive values, SEPARATION implies equality of false positive rates, and both hold together only if recidivism rates and score distributions are the same across racial groups, or some group never experiences an outcome at all
